blocks.raw: <Callout>Anthropometrics is the scientific measurement of the human body and its relationship to architectural space. The LEA tests your knowledge of three major systems—Neufert's Architects' Data, Henry Dreyfuss's The Measure of Man, and Le Corbusier's Modulor—and their specific numerical dimensions used in design. You must know standard door heights (2100mm), passage widths (900mm minimum), counter heights (900mm), and eye heights (seated ~1100–1200mm, standing ~1500–1600mm) because these appear as MCQ choices.</Callout>

blocks.raw: <Note>**Anthropometrics is not arbitrary**—it's evidence-based science linking human body dimensions to design outcomes. Buildings that ignore these standards create user frustration, safety problems, and liability. Compliance with anthropometric standards is essential, not optional.</Note>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeList mistakes={["Applying Modulor as a strict ergonomic system. The Modulor is proportional and aesthetic, not purely ergonomic. It harmonizes space but does not optimize comfort in the way Neufert or Dreyfuss does. A student might assume Modulor dimensions are \"safer\" for all design contexts, missing that Neufert and Dreyfuss are more directly linked to safety and accessibility.", "Misremembering Modulor's primary dimension. Le Corbusier's standard man is 1.83m (or 183cm), not 1.7m or 1.8m. Students under pressure often round, creating wrong answers. The 1.83m dimension is tested directly because it generates the entire proportional series.", "Treating eye height as a static dimension. Eye height varies by posture, head tilt, seating depth, and footwear. Seated eye height ~1100–1200mm is a range, not a fixed point. Students must understand that anthropometric data represents statistical central tendency, not absolutes.", "Forgetting cultural and regional variation. Anthropometric standards are based on specific populations (Neufert on European data, Dreyfuss on North American data). The Philippines may have different average heights and proportions. However, the LEA uses international (Neufert, Dreyfuss, Le Corbusier) standards as the canon, so students must master those first."]} />
